n: Baasha, king of Israel, fortified Ramah, just five miles north of Jerusalem, to blockade Judah and stop people from crossing over to Asa.

f.g: A town on the main road north of Jerusalem.

n: Instead of praying as he had against Zerah, Asa took silver and gold from the temple and palace treasuries and sent them to Ben-hadad, king of Syria in Damascus.
Asa asked Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Israel and ally with Judah instead, so Baasha would be forced to withdraw.
Ben-hadad agreed and attacked Israel’s northern towns — Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and Naphtali’s supply cities.

f.g: Also called Abel-beth-maachah, in the far north.

n: Hearing this, Baasha stopped building Ramah. Asa’s plan seemed to work — on the surface.
Asa had Judah haul away Ramah’s stones and timber to fortify Geba and Mizpah for Judah’s own defense.
The seer Hanani rebuked Asa: because you relied on Syria instead of the Lord, you lost the chance to defeat Syria too.
Hanani reminds Asa of his own past: when you faced the huge Cushite and Libyan armies and trusted the Lord, He gave you victory. Why trust a pagan king now?
A beloved verse: God’s eyes search the whole earth to show His strength for those whose hearts are fully His. Asa acted foolishly, so from now on he would have wars.

f.w: the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth

n: Instead of repenting, Asa became furious, threw the prophet into prison (literally into the stocks), and mistreated some of the people. Pride turned a good king harsh.

f.g: Literally ‘house of the stocks’ — a place of confinement and torture.

n: Asa’s full history was recorded in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
In his thirty-ninth year Asa developed a severe foot disease. Even then he sought only doctors, not the Lord. The point is not that medicine is wrong, but that he left God out entirely.

f.g: Possibly healers who used magical or pagan practices, as well as ordinary doctors.

f.w: he sought not to the LORD

n: Asa died in his forty-first year as king.
He was buried in a tomb he had prepared in the City of David, laid on a bier filled with spices and perfumes, and honored with a great memorial fire (not cremation).

f.g: A large ceremonial fire of spices in his honor.
